lesson.menu_desc: The timed pitch -- what goes first, what goes last, and what people remember -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- Introducing Yourself in Thirty Seconds
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Liliane Meira | Lesson 13 -- Introducing Yourself in Thirty Seconds
lesson.grammar_point: cleft sentences and information order (what I do is, it was... who)

listenings.text: I run a gallery booth at three art fairs a year, and on a busy day I hear perhaps a hundred introductions. Most of them start in the wrong place. People begin with their education, their first exhibition, the city they live in, and by the time they reach the work, I have stopped listening. What I remember at the end of the day is the two or three people who started with the work itself. One woman last year said: what I make are sound pieces from hospital wards. That was her whole first sentence, and I asked her three questions. The other thing that works is a single takeaway. Not five ideas. One. And please do not ramble because you are nervous. Thirty seconds is enough, if you get to the point. It is the person who stops talking first who usually gets the second conversation.

I coach researchers and artists who have to present their work in English, and the problem is almost never vocabulary. It is the order of the information. In English, the end of the sentence is where the listener expects the important part. So if you say, my work is about memory, illness, the body and care, the listener receives a list, but not the point. Compare that with: what holds all my work together is care. Now the important word arrives last, and it lands. Another tool is the sentence that begins with it was. It was a nurse who changed my project. You are telling the listener: of all the people, notice this one. These structures are not decoration. They are how you tell somebody which word to remember. Use them once or twice in a short introduction, and you come across as somebody who knows exactly what she does.
